events.text: Confidential Northwind figures: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.6/100,000 last year; Hearth 10 is 6.2% failing the 55°C test and has 6.4 thermal incidents/100,000. Three thermal incidents went unreported to any regulator. Only 38% of installed units support remote shut-off; suppression costs $42/unit; cash runway is 9 months. CEO’s priority is to avoid a binding 5% model failure cap. Red lines: no public per-model failure-rate disclosure; no retrofit shut-off deadline under 6 years. In S2, seek a staged/improvement-based requirement and confidential regulator access to per-model results, rather than public release or an immediate market ban.

Halcyon figures: overall thermal incidents 8.1/100k last year; 4 thermal incidents were not reported to regulators; flagship 55°C test failure rate 3.9%; flagship incident rate 9.9/100k; 81% of installed units support remote shut-off; built-in suppression costs $67/unit; cash runway 14 months. Red lines: customers must receive per-model test results; no new-unit suppression requirement taking effect sooner than 36 months after adoption. CEO wants S5 recall rules loose, since the Ember 8 exceeds the proposed 8/100k trigger.

For evidence-based drafting, please share your relevant figures for the sections under discussion—especially incident/reporting data, per-model 55°C test and incident rates, remote shut-off coverage, and suppression costs. We can compare evidence before proposing thresholds and timelines.

Northwind figures relevant to the requested sections: 8.6 company-wide thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year; three thermal incidents were not reported to any regulator; Hearth 10 has a 6.2% failure rate in the 55°C sustained-heat test and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 units; 38% of installed units support remote emergency shut-off; built-in suppression costs $42 per unit. These are company-reported figures for discussion.

## S1_incident_reporting
Manufacturers shall report to the relevant regulator any battery-related fire, thermal runaway, or overheating event requiring emergency-service response, causing injury or property damage, or requiring evacuation, within 24 hours of learning of it. Other confirmed thermal incidents shall be reported within 5 business days. Reports shall include known circumstances, affected model and serial/batch information, and actions taken; updates shall be provided as material facts emerge. Manufacturers shall notify affected customers within 5 business days of confirming a safety risk that could require a change in use or service, and immediately where continued use presents an imminent serious risk. Regulators may require prompt customer notice where needed to protect the public.

## S2_thermal_testing
Each model shall undergo a standardized sustained-heat test at 55°C before initial market placement and after a material design or manufacturing change, using a statistically adequate sample and a published test protocol. Manufacturers shall submit per-model test results, sample size, and corrective-action plans to the regulator; results shall not require public disclosure of individual-company per-model failure rates. A result above the 5% benchmark triggers regulator review and a corrective-action plan with retesting on a regulator-approved schedule. The benchmark is a safety trigger for review and remediation, not by itself an automatic market ban; regulators may impose proportionate measures based on the evidence and risk.

Each model shall undergo a standardized sustained-heat test at 55°C before initial market placement and after a material design or manufacturing change, using a statistically adequate sample and a published test protocol. Manufacturers shall submit per-model test results, sample size, and corrective-action plans to the regulator, and shall provide the results for a model to customers who buy that model, including prospective buyers before purchase. A result above the 5% benchmark triggers regulator review and a corrective-action plan with retesting on a regulator-approved schedule. The benchmark is a safety trigger for review and remediation, not by itself an automatic market ban; regulators may impose proportionate measures based on evidence and risk.

New home battery units shall include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers shall disclose compliance status and any interim risk-reduction measures to regulators and customers. The transition period does not limit regulators’ authority to require earlier measures for a specific model where evidence indicates an imminent serious risk.

Customers shall receive clear safety notices promptly when a manufacturer or regulator identifies a safety risk that could affect use, maintenance, or continued operation; notices shall explain the risk and required actions. A recall is mandatory when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period. Manufacturers shall promptly notify regulators and affected customers, stop sale of the affected model pending corrective action, and provide a repair, replacement, or refund plan. Regulators may require additional measures where the evidence indicates serious risk, even below the threshold.

New home battery units shall support a remotely initiated emergency shut-off no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard. For units already installed, manufacturers shall provide remote shut-off capability through retrofit or replacement within 6 years after adoption, where technically feasible. Manufacturers shall submit implementation plans and progress reports to regulators. Regulators may require earlier action for a specific model where evidence indicates an imminent serious risk.

Northwind supports S2 treating 5% as a review and remediation benchmark, not a binding pass/fail market-access limit. Any corrective action or restriction should be proportionate to the evidence and risk, with no automatic ban solely for exceeding the benchmark. Per-model results should remain with regulators and relevant customers, not be publicly published.

Customers shall receive clear safety notices promptly when a manufacturer or regulator identifies a safety risk that could affect use, maintenance, or continued operation; notices shall explain the risk and required actions. When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a 12-month period, the manufacturer shall promptly notify regulators and submit the incident data and a corrective-action plan for review. The threshold triggers a regulator risk assessment, not an automatic recall or stop-sale. Regulators may require a recall, stop-sale, or other proportionate measures based on evidence of risk, including below the threshold.

I propose treating 8 incidents per 100,000 as a mandatory reporting and regulator-review trigger rather than an automatic recall. A single rate threshold can prompt investigation and corrective action, while recall and stop-sale decisions should reflect the evidence and severity of risk. This preserves prompt regulator and customer protections without making the threshold an automatic market ban.
